unit.title: Weld using submerged arc welding process

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In submerged arc welding (SAW), where is the arc?
options: Inside a shield of argon gas from a nozzle
Between a tungsten rod and the plate
Hidden under a layer of granular flux
Inside a hollow wire packed with flux

questions.stem: Why is SAW mainly used for flat welds and horizontal fillets?
options: The loose flux and big pool would fall away in other positions
The wire cannot be bent to reach a vertical or overhead joint
The flux only melts when it lies on a flat, level surface
The machine is far too heavy to be held in any other position

questions.stem: Which job suits SAW best?
options: A small repair to a car exhaust pipe
Overhead site welds on a light handrail
Tack welds on thin sheet metal ducting
Long straight seams on a thick tank shell

questions.stem: Compared with MMAW, what is the main advantage of SAW on suitable work?
options: It can be used in every position on site
It lays far more weld metal, in long, even runs
It needs no joint preparation, even on very thick plate
It needs no checks because it is automatic

questions.stem: Why do SAW operators still need eye protection, although the arc is covered by flux?
options: The arc can flash through if the flux runs thin
The flux gives off a bright light when cold
The wire glows white-hot all along the reel as it feeds
The rollers throw sparks every time they turn

questions.stem: What is the main breathing hazard when filling hoppers and sieving SAW flux for reuse?
options: Ozone from the arc light
Argon leaking from the nozzle
Fine flux dust in the air
Steam from the cooling water

questions.stem: SAW slag often peels off the seam in a long, hot strip. What is the main danger?
options: It is sharp but cold, so only cuts are a risk
It is very hot and can burn skin or start a fire
It gives off a toxic gas as soon as it cools
It is magnetic and will jump to the welder's tools

questions.stem: On a SAW tractor, what keeps the wire on the joint line along a long seam?
options: The operator's hand held on the torch the whole time
The flux pressing the wire down into the groove
The magnetic pull of the arc on the plate edges
A guide or seam tracker set before the run starts

questions.stem: What is a column and boom used for in SAW?
options: To hold and move the welding head over large work
To store spare coils of wire off the floor
To lift the finished tanks onto the delivery truck safely
To hold the flux recovery bags above the job

questions.stem: For a circumferential seam on a tank, how is the work usually moved under a fixed SAW head?
options: It is pulled along the floor by the crane
It is pushed round by hand with bars
It is turned on powered turning rolls
It is not moved; the head goes round it

questions.stem: When welding the outside of a turning cylinder with SAW, why is the wire set a short distance off top dead centre, as the WPS says?
options: So the flux can be poured in more easily
So the pool freezes near the top and does not run off
So the slag falls cleanly onto the turning rolls below the job
So the operator can see the arc from the side

questions.stem: For storage, what is the main difference between fused and agglomerated (bonded) SAW fluxes?
options: Fused flux must always be kept in a hot oven
Bonded flux can be left open in the yard
Both are the same and need no special care
Bonded flux picks up moisture more easily

questions.stem: A bag of agglomerated flux has been left open in the humid workshop for a week. What should be done before it is used?
options: Use it at once, before it gets any damper
Mix it half and half with new flux from a bag
Re-dry it as the maker says, or scrap it
Spread it thin on the plate to dry in the sun

questions.stem: In a SAW wire-flux classification such as F7A2-EM12K, what does the first letter "F" show?
options: Flux
Fillet
Flat
Fused

questions.stem: In F7A2-EM12K, what does the "A" after the 7 show?
options: The weld was tested after heat treatment
The weld was tested as-welded
The flux is for AC welding only
The flux is the agglomerated type

questions.stem: In the SAW wire class EM12K, what does the "K" show?
options: The wire is coated with copper
The wire is 12 mm across
The wire is for thick plate only
The wire is made from killed steel

questions.stem: In SAW, which setting mainly controls how deep the weld penetrates?
options: The arc voltage
The flux depth
The welding current
The wire diameter

questions.stem: The arc voltage in SAW is raised, with the other settings the same. What mainly happens?
options: The bead gets narrower and much deeper
The bead gets wider and flatter, and more flux is used
The current doubles and the wire burns back
Nothing changes, as voltage has no effect at all in the SAW process

questions.stem: The travel speed is raised, with the same current and voltage. What happens to the bead?
options: It gets smaller and narrower
It gets wider and much taller
It gets deeper and hotter
It stays exactly the same

questions.stem: What happens if the wire stick-out in SAW is made much longer, with the same settings?
options: Less wire melts, and penetration gets deeper
The arc goes out because the wire is too far away
The flux melts faster than the wire does
More wire melts, with less penetration

questions.stem: What happens if the flux layer over the SAW arc is too shallow?
options: The weld runs cooler and penetrates much deeper into the plate
The arc flashes through and the weld may be porous
The slag becomes too thick to remove
The wire stops feeding into the joint

questions.stem: A SAW bead comes out rough and pock-marked, though the plate and wire are clean. The flux pile is very deep. What is the likely cause?
options: The wire is too thin for the job
The plate is too thick for the current
Gas cannot escape through the deep flux
The tractor is running too slowly

questions.stem: Which polarity is most often used for single-wire SAW on carbon steel?
options: DC electrode positive
DC electrode negative
High-frequency AC
Pulsed DC only

questions.stem: Why is AC sometimes chosen for SAW at very high currents or for the second head of a tandem set?
options: AC gives much deeper penetration than DC
AC needs no flux, so it saves on cost
AC lets the wire feed faster than DC
AC reduces arc blow from magnetic fields

questions.stem: Why are run-on and run-off tabs fitted at the ends of a SAW seam?
options: So the seam can be lifted by its ends
So the plate does not distort at the ends
So the start and the crater are made off the job
So the inspector can stamp the welder's mark

questions.stem: A one-sided SAW butt with full penetration needs support under the root. Which is commonly used?
options: A wooden plank wedged under the joint
A copper bar, a flux bed or a steel backing strip
A sheet of cardboard taped under the seam
Nothing at all, as SAW never burns through the root of a joint

questions.stem: Why must tack welds for a SAW seam be small, sound and well fused?
options: The SAW pass must melt them in fully, or faults stay
So the inspector does not see them in the report
So they can be broken off easily after the SAW pass is finished
So the flux sticks to them and stays in place

questions.stem: Why is SAW less forgiving of an uneven root gap than a skilled manual welder?
options: The flux fills the gap before the wire arrives
The machine runs too slowly for wide gaps
The wire is too thick to enter a narrow gap
The machine cannot change its speed to suit the gap

questions.stem: A SAW butt weld in thick plate has a crack along its centre. The bead is deeper than it is wide. Which change helps most?
options: Raise the current to melt the crack closed
Use a deeper flux layer over the arc
Make the bead wider than it is deep
Weld faster with a longer stick-out

questions.stem: What most often causes porosity in a SAW weld?
options: Too shallow a groove angle on the plate
Damp flux, or rust and oil on the joint
Too much current on the second pass
Turning rolls that run a little fast

questions.stem: Slag is found trapped between passes along one side wall of a multi-pass SAW joint. What is the most likely cause?
options: Slag left in a notch at the side of the pass before
Flux that was too dry when it was poured
A run-off tab fitted at the end of the seam
Too slow a turning speed set on the rolls under the vessel shell

questions.stem: A SAW fillet weld shows undercut along both toes. What is a likely cause?
options: Too low a voltage and too slow a travel speed
Flux that has been sieved and passed over a magnet
A run-on tab that was too long
Travel speed or voltage set too high

questions.stem: A tee joint is tilted to 45° so that its fillet is welded in the flat (1F) position with SAW. What does this mainly give?
options: Less flux used and a lighter slag
Equal legs and deep, even penetration
A narrower bead with more undercut
A weld that needs no inspection

questions.stem: Why is recovered SAW flux sieved and passed over a magnet before it is used again?
options: To warm it up before it goes back in the hopper
To make the flux grains smaller and finer
To remove slag lumps, scale and bits of metal
To mix it with the wire offcuts for strength

questions.stem: Why should fine dust not be allowed to build up in recycled flux?
options: Too many fines can trap gas and spoil the bead
Fine dust makes the arc burn much hotter
Fines make the slag too easy to remove
Fine dust stops the wire from feeding

questions.stem: Which document gives the wire, flux, current, voltage, travel speed and stick-out for a SAW joint?
options: The label on the bag of flux
The machine's rating plate
The supplier's delivery note
The WPS for that joint

questions.stem: The WPS names a certain wire-flux combination. The store offers a different flux that looks the same. What should happen?
options: Use it, as all SAW fluxes give the same weld
Use it only if the WPS covers it, or requalify
Mix it with the old flux to be safe
Use it, but raise the current by 10%

questions.stem: A SAW pass is run at 32 V and 600 A at 480 mm/min. Taking heat input as V × A × 60 ÷ (speed × 1000), what is it?
options: 1.2 kJ/mm
1.8 kJ/mm
2.4 kJ/mm
24 kJ/mm

questions.stem: A tank has 4 seams, each 3 m long. Each seam needs 2 SAW passes on each side, at 500 mm/min. What is the total arc time?
options: 24 minutes
48 minutes
72 minutes
96 minutes

questions.stem: A SAW head deposits about 8 kg of weld metal per hour of arc time. A joint needs 20 kg. How many hours of arc time is that?
options: 2.5 hours
1.6 hours
4.0 hours
12 hours

questions.stem: A job will use 40 kg of SAW wire. The flux used is about 1.2 kg for each kg of wire. About how much flux is needed?
options: 33 kg
40 kg
48 kg
52 kg

questions.stem: After SAW of the seams on a pressure vessel, which tests are usually used to check inside the full weld?
options: A hammer test and a visual check
Radiography or ultrasonic testing
A paint test and a soap test
A spark test on the wire offcuts

questions.stem: Before a SAW run, the operator moves the head along the seam with the arc off. Why?
options: To warm up the motor of the tractor
To spread the flux evenly along the seam
To clean the plate with the wire tip
To check the wire follows the joint all the way

questions.stem: A new SAW operator wants to brush the flux aside during a run to look at the arc. What should you tell him?
options: Watch the meters and the bead, and keep the arc covered
Go ahead, as long as he wears dark glasses
Brush the flux aside only near the end of each run, then cover it again
Stop the run and restart it with less flux

questions.stem: SAW wire comes on 25 kg coils. What is the safe way to fit a new coil on the head?
options: Throw it up to a person standing on the head
Lift it alone, as quickly as possible
Use a lifting aid or two people, as the rules say
Roll it up a plank onto the head

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A process is shown on the WPS as SAW. What do these letters stand for?
What is the name of the granular material that covers the arc in SAW?
Name the powered rollers used to turn a cylinder under a fixed SAW head.
On a long SAW seam, what is the extra piece at the far end called, onto which the run is carried so the crater is off the job?
In the SAW class F7A2-EM12K, which half of the code describes the wire: F7A2 or EM12K?
In a SAW wire-flux class such as F7A2-EM12K, the A means tested as-welded. Which letter would show it was tested after heat treatment?
What is the name for magnetic forces pushing the arc off line, which can be a problem in SAW at high DC currents?
Which type of SAW flux, made by melting the ingredients and crushing the glassy result, picks up little moisture?
A SAW tractor travels 1.5 m in 3 minutes. What is its travel speed, in mm/min?
What name is given to the very fine dust particles that must be kept out of recycled SAW flux?
What is the name of the self-driven carriage that carries a SAW head along a track or along the plate?
What name is given to SAW in which two wires are fed one behind the other into the same pool?
What is the name of the container on a SAW head that holds a stock of flux and feeds it to the joint?
A seam is 4 m long and is welded at 400 mm/min. How many minutes of arc time does one pass take?
What is the AWS position code for a fillet weld made in the horizontal position, such as a SAW fillet on a beam web?

essays.stem: Explain how submerged arc welding works, and compare it with MMAW and FCAW for welding long seams in thick plate. Give its main advantages and its limits.
essays.modelAnswer: In SAW a bare wire is fed by a motor through a contact tip into the joint, and the arc burns under a layer of granular flux fed from a hopper. Part of the flux melts to form slag that protects and shapes the weld, and the rest is recovered. The head is carried by a tractor, a column and boom, or the work is turned on rolls. Compared with MMAW and FCAW, SAW lays down far more weld metal per hour, gives deep penetration and smooth, even welds with little spatter, smoke or arc light, and needs fewer passes on thick plate. Its limits are that it works only in the flat position and for horizontal fillets, it needs accurate fit-up and tracking because it cannot adjust itself, the equipment is costly and heavy, and it does not suit short or awkward joints or site work in every position. It is best for long, straight or round seams in shop production.
markingPoints: Describes the process: wire fed under granular flux, slag, flux recovery
Describes how the head or work is moved
Advantages: high deposition, deep penetration, smooth welds, little light and fume
Limits: flat and horizontal only, needs accurate fit-up and tracking, costly equipment
Clear comparison with MMAW and FCAW and the jobs SAW suits

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up a SAW tractor to weld a long butt seam in thick plate, from reading the WPS to starting the first run.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the WPS for the wire, flux, polarity, current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out and pass plan, and check the plate edges and fit-up: clean, dry, even gap and tacks sound. I fit run-on and run-off tabs of the same steel at each end. I lay the track parallel to the seam, or set the guide wheel or seam tracker, and do a dry run with the arc off to check the wire stays on the joint line the whole length. I check the wire is the right class and size, the drive rolls and contact tip match, and the flux in the hopper is the right type, dry and free of lumps. I connect the work lead close to the seam to cut arc blow. I set the stick-out and the flux depth so the arc will be fully covered, set the parameters, and check the readings on a test run on a scrap plate before starting on the run-on tab.
markingPoints: Reads the WPS and checks joint preparation, fit-up and tacks
Fits run-on and run-off tabs
Sets track, guide or seam tracker, and does a dry run
Checks wire, tip, drive rolls, flux type and dryness; work lead placement
Sets stick-out, flux depth and parameters; test run before starting on the run-on tab

essays.stem: Explain how welding current, arc voltage, travel speed and wire stick-out each affect the shape and penetration of a SAW bead.
essays.modelAnswer: Welding current is the main control of penetration and melting rate. More current gives deeper penetration and more weld metal, but too much can burn through or give a deep, narrow bead that cracks along its centre. Arc voltage sets the arc length and mainly controls the bead width. Higher voltage gives a wider, flatter bead and melts more flux, but too high can cause undercut and an uneven bead; too low gives a tall, narrow bead. Travel speed controls the bead size. Faster travel gives a smaller, narrower bead with less penetration and can leave undercut; slower travel gives a large bead and a big pool that may run ahead or give poor fusion. A longer wire stick-out heats the wire more before it reaches the arc, so more wire melts and the deposit goes up, but penetration goes down. All four are set within the WPS ranges and checked during the run.
markingPoints: Current: penetration and melting rate; risks of too much
Voltage: bead width and flatness, flux use; too high or too low
Travel speed: bead size and penetration; undercut or large pool
Stick-out: more deposit, less penetration
Settings kept within the WPS and checked

essays.stem: Describe the main types of SAW flux, and explain how flux should be stored, dried, recovered and recycled, and why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Fused flux is made by melting the ingredients and crushing the glassy result. It picks up little moisture and gives few fines. Agglomerated, or bonded, flux is made by bonding fine powders into grains. It can carry alloying elements, but it picks up moisture more easily. Flux is stored sealed in a dry store, off the floor, and opened bags are kept in a heated flux oven or hopper if the maker says so. Damp flux is re-dried at the temperature and time the maker gives, because moisture causes porosity and hydrogen cracking. After welding, unfused flux is recovered by vacuum or sweeping, then sieved to remove slag lumps and passed over a magnet to remove scale and metal. Fines are removed and new flux is mixed in as the maker advises, because too many fines trap gas and spoil the bead. The flux type and batch are recorded so they can be traced.
markingPoints: Describes fused and agglomerated flux and their moisture behaviour
Dry, sealed storage, heated oven where needed
Re-drying damp flux, with the reason (porosity, hydrogen)
Recovery: sieving, magnet, removing fines, topping up with new flux
Records of flux type and batch

essays.stem: Explain the causes and cures for centreline cracking, porosity, slag inclusions and undercut in SAW welds.
essays.modelAnswer: Centreline cracking happens when the bead is deeper than it is wide, often from high current in a narrow groove, or from high restraint and impurities. The cure is to make the bead wider than it is deep by lowering the current, raising the voltage, or opening the groove, and to follow any preheat. Porosity comes from damp flux, rust, oil, paint or primer on the joint, too shallow a flux layer, or too many fines. The cure is dry flux, clean joints and the correct flux depth. Slag inclusions come from slag left between passes, often in notches along the side walls, or a wrong wire position. The cure is full cleaning, placing passes so they wet the side walls, and grinding notches. Undercut comes from too high a travel speed or voltage, or a wrongly aimed wire. The cure is to reduce speed or voltage and check the wire position, keeping within the WPS.
markingPoints: Centreline cracking: deep narrow bead or restraint; cure by bead shape and preheat
Porosity: damp flux, dirty joints, shallow flux, fines; cures
Slag inclusions: poor cleaning, notches, wire position; cures
Undercut: high speed or voltage, wire aim; cures
Cures kept within the WPS

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of submerged arc welding in a fabrication shop and the controls you would use for each.
essays.modelAnswer: SAW uses very high currents, so cables, connections and the work return are checked, and the set is isolated before tips or wire are changed. The arc can flash through thin flux, so the operator wears suitable eye protection and keeps the flux topped up. Flux dust from filling hoppers and recycling can harm the lungs, so dust is kept down, recovery systems are used and a dust mask is worn as the SDS says. The slag comes off very hot, so gloves and long sleeves are worn, the slag is put in a metal bin and anything that burns is kept away. The weld and plate stay hot for a long time and are marked. Turning rolls and moving tractors can trap hands and clothing, so guards, stop buttons and clear walkways are needed. Coils of wire and bags of flux are heavy, so lifting aids are used. All work follows the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Electrical: high current, checks, isolation
Arc flash-through: eye protection, flux depth
Flux dust: dust control, recovery, mask per SDS
Hot slag and plate; moving rolls and tractors (guards, stops, clear walkways)
Manual handling of coils and flux; maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: Explain how a circumferential seam on a steel tank is welded with SAW on turning rolls, including the set-up of the rolls, the wire position, the travel speed and the checks made.
essays.modelAnswer: The tank is placed on turning rolls set to the right spacing for its diameter, and checked so it turns evenly without creeping along the rolls. The head is set on a column and boom over the seam. The wire is set a short distance off top dead centre, as the WPS says, so the pool freezes as it reaches the top and does not run off; on an inside seam the offset is the other way. The surface speed of the rolls gives the travel speed, so it is set and checked by timing a marked length round the shell. The work lead is fitted with a rotating earth clamp. A dry run checks the wire follows the seam all the way round. During welding the operator watches the meters, the flux cover and the tracking, and adjusts the head if the seam wanders. Where the end of the run meets the start, the overlap is controlled to avoid a crater, and the seam is cleaned and inspected.
markingPoints: Turning rolls set for the diameter; tank turns evenly
Wire set off top dead centre as the WPS says, with the reason
Travel speed from roll surface speed, checked by timing
Rotating earth, dry run and tracking during the run
Start-stop overlap controlled; clean and inspect

essays.stem: Explain how a SAW welding procedure is qualified to the code the Centre uses, and which changes on a job would need a new or re-qualified procedure.
essays.modelAnswer: A draft procedure is written for the plate, joint, wire-flux combination, polarity, current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out, passes, preheat and interpass. A test plate is welded to it while an inspector records the actual values. It is inspected visually and often by radiography or ultrasonics, then test pieces are cut for tensile, bend and sometimes impact and macro tests. If they pass, the results go on the procedure qualification record and the WPS is issued with limits from it. Changes that usually need a new or re-qualified procedure include a different wire-flux classification, a change in flux type, a change from one wire to two wires, a change in polarity or from DC to AC, a large change in heat input, a different joint design or backing, a new material group, or a change to preheat. The team leader checks every change against the WPS before work goes on.
markingPoints: Draft procedure with the main variables
Test plate welded with values recorded
NDT and mechanical tests named
PQR and WPS limits
Examples of changes that need requalification (wire-flux, wires, polarity, heat input, joint, material)

essays.stem: You are in charge of the SAW welding of the shell seams of six water tanks for a parish council in Clarendon. Explain how you would plan, run and check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the drawings and specification, confirm the approved WPS for each seam and check the operators are trained and qualified for SAW. I would check the plates, wire and flux against the WPS, with the flux stored dry and a flux log kept. I would plan the order: longitudinal seams first, then circumferential seams on the rolls, with the run-on and run-off tabs, the track or column set-up, and the time needed, using arc time worked out from the seam lengths and travel speed. I would brief the team on the set-up, roles, hold points and safety, including moving rolls and flux dust. The first seam would be inspected before the rest. During the work I would check fit-up, tracking, settings, flux depth and cleaning between passes. Each seam would be numbered with the operator, wire and flux batches, and inspection results. Repairs would follow procedure and be re-inspected before the tanks are released.
markingPoints: Confirms WPS, specification and operator qualification
Checks materials and flux control
Plans order, set-up and time, with arc time worked out
Briefs the team; first-off inspection and checks during work
Records each seam; repairs re-inspected before release

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out the arc time, wire and flux needed for a SAW job, and how you would use the figures to plan the work. Use a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the total length of weld: each seam's length times the number of passes. Arc time is that length divided by the travel speed. For example, 4 seams of 3 m, each with 4 passes, is 48 m of weld. At 500 mm/min (0.5 m/min) that is 96 minutes of arc time. Wire is found from the weld metal needed. If the joint needs 20 kg of weld metal, SAW puts nearly all the wire into the weld, so I order about 20 kg plus an allowance for waste, say 22 kg. If flux is used at about 1.2 kg per kg of wire, about 26 kg of flux is needed, less what is recovered. To plan, I add set-up, tracking checks, cleaning between passes, cooling and inspection to the arc time, because arc time is only a part of the job. These figures let me book the machine, order wire and flux, and give the client a realistic time.
markingPoints: Total weld length from seams times passes
Arc time from length ÷ travel speed, worked correctly
Wire from weld metal needed, with an allowance
Flux from the flux-to-wire ratio, less recovery
Adds non-arc time to plan the job, order materials and give a time

practical1.title: Set up and run a SAW butt seam with run-on and run-off tabs (or a full set-up check if the Centre has no SAW machine)
practical1.brief: The Centre may not have a submerged arc machine, so this task has two forms; the assessor tells the group which one it will do. Form A (the Centre has a SAW machine): with the assessor's WPS for a butt seam in carbon steel plate (about 10–12 mm, welded from both sides or on a backing bar), the group prepares and tacks the plates, fits run-on and run-off tabs, lays the track or sets the guide, does a dry run, checks the flux is dry, and sets the stick-out, flux depth and parameters. Members take turns in each role: operator, flux and hopper, tracking and meters, and recorder, so that every member operates for at least one run. Form B (no SAW machine): the group does the same set-up on a travel carriage or cutting tractor on its track, with the arc never struck: tack the plates and tabs, align the track, do the dry run, measure and record the carriage speed by timing a marked length, set a stick-out and a flux depth with dry flux if the Centre has some, and complete the set-up checklist. If the assessor arranges a visit to a shop that uses SAW, the group may instead record a full set-up there, with the shop's permission. In both forms, write the settings and checks on the record sheet and photograph each stage.
materials: SAW WPS and set-up checklist (from the assessor)
Carbon steel plates bevelled or square-edged to the WPS, with run-on and run-off tabs
Form A: SAW machine (tractor or head on a column and boom), wire and flux to the WPS
Form B: a travel carriage or cutting tractor with its track; dry flux if available
Stopwatch, steel rule, tape measure and a flux scoop
Grinder, tack welding set, chipping hammer and wire brush
photos: The plates tacked with run-on and run-off tabs fitted
The track or guide set along the seam, with the dry run in progress
The stick-out being measured and the flux depth set
Form A: the finished seam with the slag removed; Form B: the carriage speed being timed
The completed record sheet and checklist
The area cleaned, with flux recovered and stored
checklist: Read the WPS and set or recorded the settings within its ranges
Prepared and tacked the plates, with sound tacks and tabs fitted
Aligned the track or guide and carried out a dry run along the full seam
Checked the flux was the right type and dry, and set the stick-out and flux depth
Form A: operated the machine for a run while watching meters, flux cover and tracking; Form B: measured travel speed correctly
Recorded the settings and checks accurately
Recovered and stored flux and cleared the area safely
safety: Wear eye protection near a SAW run in case of flash-through
Wear a dust mask when filling hoppers or handling flux, as the SDS says
Treat slag and plate as hot; put slag in a metal bin
Keep hands and clothing clear of moving carriages and rolls; know the stop button
Use a lifting aid or two people for wire coils and flux bags

practical2.title: Write a SAW procedure, job plan and flux control sheet for the shell seams of a water tank
practical2.brief: This task is done on paper and does not need a SAW machine. The assessor gives the group a drawing of a small steel water tank (shell plates, seam lengths and plate thickness), a wire and flux data sheet and a blank WPS form. As a group, share out the work so that each member writes one part and checks another member's part: (1) a draft SAW WPS for the longitudinal seam: joint design, backing or back weld, wire-flux classification, polarity, current, voltage, travel speed, stick-out, flux depth and pass plan; (2) the arc time, wire and flux needed for all the shell seams, with the working shown; (3) a set-up plan for the circumferential seam on turning rolls, including the wire offset from top dead centre and how the travel speed will be checked; (4) a flux control sheet: storage, re-drying, recovery, sieving and records; (5) an inspection and safety checklist for the job. Present the pack to the assessor, with each member explaining their part. Photograph each part as it is finished.
materials: Tank drawing, wire and flux data sheet and blank WPS form (from the assessor)
